cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
In compact predictor notation (Eq. 4.112–4.113), the one-step-ahead predictor is written as $\hat{y}(t|t-1) = W(q)z(t)$, where:
$$W(q) = {{c1::[W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]}} \quad \text{and} \quad z(t) = \begin{bmatrix} u(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}$$
cards.raw_back: The $1 \times 2$ predictor filter matrix operating on the observed input-output data vector $z(t)$.
cards.anki_front:
In compact predictor notation (Eq. 4.112–4.113), the one-step-ahead predictor is written as \(\hat{y}(t|t-1) = W(q)z(t)\), where:

\(W(q) =\) {{c1::\([W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]\)}} \(\quad \text{and} \quad z(t) = \begin{bmatrix} u(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix} \)
cards.anki_back: The \(1 \times 2\) predictor filter matrix operating on the observed input-output data vector \(z(t)\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
How are the components of the one-step-ahead predictor filter $W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]$ expressed in terms of the system transfer functions $T(q) = [G(q) \quad H(q)]$ (Eq. 4.114)?
$$W_u(q) = {{c1::H^{-1}(q)G(q)}}, \qquad W_y(q) = {{c1::1 - H^{-1}(q)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Derived directly from the one-step-ahead predictor $\hat{y}(t|t-1) = H^{-1}(q)G(q)u(t) + [1 - H^{-1}(q)]y(t)$.
cards.anki_front:
How are the components of the one-step-ahead predictor filter \(W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]\) expressed in terms of the system transfer functions \(T(q) = [G(q) \quad H(q)]\) (Eq. 4.114)?

\(W_u(q) =\) {{c1::\(H^{-1}(q)G(q)\)}} \(, \qquad W_y(q) =\) {{c1::\(1 - H^{-1}(q)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Derived directly from the one-step-ahead predictor \(\hat{y}(t|t-1) = H^{-1}(q)G(q)u(t) + [1 - H^{-1}(q)]y(t)\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
Given the one-step-ahead predictor filter $W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]$, how do you invert the one-to-one mapping $T(q) \leftrightarrow W(q)$ (Eq. 4.114–4.115) to recover $H(q)$ and $G(q)$?
$$H(q) = {{c1::[1 - W_y(q)]^{-1}}}, \qquad G(q) = {{c1::[1 - W_y(q)]^{-1}W_u(q)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Since $W_y(q) = 1 - H^{-1}(q)$ and $W_u(q) = H^{-1}(q)G(q)$, solving for $H(q)$ and $G(q)$ establishes a bijection $T(q) \leftrightarrow W(q)$ whenever $H(q)$ is monic ($H(\infty)=1$).
cards.anki_front:
Given the one-step-ahead predictor filter \(W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]\), how do you invert the one-to-one mapping \(T(q) \leftrightarrow W(q)\) (Eq. 4.114–4.115) to recover \(H(q)\) and \(G(q)\)?

\(H(q) =\) {{c1::\([1 - W_y(q)]^{-1} \)}} \(, \qquad G(q) =\) {{c1::\([1 - W_y(q)]^{-1}W_u(q)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Since \(W_y(q) = 1 - H^{-1}(q)\) and \(W_u(q) = H^{-1}(q)G(q)\), solving for \(H(q)\) and \(G(q)\) establishes a bijection \(T(q) \leftrightarrow W(q)\) whenever \(H(q)\) is monic (\(H(\infty)=1\)).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: Even though $T(q) = [G(q) \;\; H(q)]$ and $W(q) = [W_u(q) \;\; W_y(q)]$ are in a one-to-one relationship (Eq. 4.115) for linear time-invariant models, why does Ljung relax this link and define the predictor filter $W(q)$ as the fundamental basic model?
cards.raw_back:
1. **What matters in the end is prediction**: System identification evaluates models by how they predict future outputs from observed data $z(t) = [u(t) \;\; y(t)]^T$.
2. **Deterministic validity**: Predictor models are completely meaningful in a purely deterministic framework without needing a stochastic alibi ($e(t)$).
3. **Generalization**: Taking the predictor $\hat{y}(t|t-1)$ as primary allows a direct extension to nonlinear and time-varying models (Chapter 5).
cards.anki_front: Even though \(T(q) = [G(q) \;\; H(q)]\) and \(W(q) = [W_u(q) \;\; W_y(q)]\) are in a one-to-one relationship (Eq. 4.115) for linear time-invariant models, why does Ljung relax this link and define the predictor filter \(W(q)\) as the fundamental basic model?
cards.anki_back:
1. What matters in the end is prediction: System identification evaluates models by how they predict future outputs from observed data \(z(t) = [u(t) \;\; y(t)]^T\).
2. Deterministic validity: Predictor models are completely meaningful in a purely deterministic framework without needing a stochastic alibi (\(e(t)\)).
3. Generalization: Taking the predictor \(\hat{y}(t|t-1)\) as primary allows a direct extension to nonlinear and time-varying models (Chapter 5).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: **Definition 4.1 (Predictor Model)**: A *predictor model* of a linear, time-invariant system is a {{c1::stable filter $W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]$, defining a predictor $\hat{y}(t|t-1) = W(q)z(t)$}}.
cards.raw_back: Stability of both components $W_u(q)$ and $W_y(q)$ is required so that the infinite-past filtering operation $W(q)z(t)$ is well defined.
cards.anki_front: Definition 4.1 (Predictor Model): A predictor model of a linear, time-invariant system is a {{c1::stable filter \(W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]\), defining a predictor \(\hat{y}(t|t-1) = W(q)z(t)\)}}.
cards.anki_back: Stability of both components \(W_u(q)\) and \(W_y(q)\) is required so that the infinite-past filtering operation \(W(q)z(t)\) is well defined.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: In Definition 4.1 of a predictor model $W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]$, why is stability of both components of $W(q)$ strictly required?
cards.raw_back: Because the predictor $\hat{y}(t|t-1) = W(q)z(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_u(k)u(t-k) + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_y(k)y(t-k)$ is an infinite-past convolution; stability ($\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} |w(k)| < \infty$) is necessary for the right-hand side of $\hat{y}(t|t-1) = W(q)z(t)$ to be well defined and computable from finite-window data.
cards.anki_front: In Definition 4.1 of a predictor model \(W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]\), why is stability of both components of \(W(q)\) strictly required?
cards.anki_back: Because the predictor \(\hat{y}(t|t-1) = W(q)z(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_u(k)u(t-k) + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_y(k)y(t-k)\) is an infinite-past convolution; stability (\(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} |w(k)| < \infty\)) is necessary for the right-hand side of \(\hat{y}(t|t-1) = W(q)z(t)\) to be well defined and computable from finite-window data.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: **Definition 4.2 (Complete Probabilistic Model)**: A *complete probabilistic model* of a linear, time-invariant system is a pair {{c1::$(W(q), f_e(x))$ consisting of a stable predictor model $W(q)$ and the probability density function $f_e(x)$ of the associated prediction errors (innovations)}}.
cards.raw_back: One can also have partially specified probabilistic models where $f_e(x)$ is only specified up to its second moment (variance $\lambda$ of $e$).
cards.anki_front: Definition 4.2 (Complete Probabilistic Model): A complete probabilistic model of a linear, time-invariant system is a pair {{c1::\((W(q), f_e(x))\) consisting of a stable predictor model \(W(q)\) and the probability density function \(f_e(x)\) of the associated prediction errors (innovations)}}.
cards.anki_back: One can also have partially specified probabilistic models where \(f_e(x)\) is only specified up to its second moment (variance \(\lambda\) of \(e\)).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
When are two predictor models $W_1(q)$ and $W_2(q)$ defined to be *equal* (Eq. 4.116)?
$$\text{If } {{c1::W_1(e^{i\omega}) = W_2(e^{i\omega}) \quad \text{for almost all } \omega}}$$
cards.raw_back: By the one-to-one correspondence $T(q) \leftrightarrow W(q)$, this is equivalent to $G_1(e^{i\omega}) = G_2(e^{i\omega})$ and $H_1(e^{i\omega}) = H_2(e^{i\omega})$ for almost all $\omega$.
cards.anki_front:
When are two predictor models \(W_1(q)\) and \(W_2(q)\) defined to be equal (Eq. 4.116)?

\(\text{If } \) {{c1::\(W_1(e^{i\omega}) = W_2(e^{i\omega}) \quad \text{for almost all } \omega\)}}
cards.anki_back: By the one-to-one correspondence \(T(q) \leftrightarrow W(q)\), this is equivalent to \(G_1(e^{i\omega}) = G_2(e^{i\omega})\) and \(H_1(e^{i\omega}) = H_2(e^{i\omega})\) for almost all \(\omega\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
A predictor model $W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]$ is called a *$k$-step-ahead predictor model* (Eq. 4.117) if $W_y(q)$ has the impulse response expansion:
$$W_y(q) = {{c1::\sum_{\ell=k}^{\infty} w_y(\ell)q^{-\ell} \quad \text{with } w_y(k) \neq 0}}$$
cards.raw_back: That is, the output feedback filter $W_y(q)$ uses only outputs up to time $t-k$ (having a delay of at least $k$ samples).
cards.anki_front:
A predictor model \(W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]\) is called a \(k\)-step-ahead predictor model (Eq. 4.117) if \(W_y(q)\) has the impulse response expansion:

\(W_y(q) =\) {{c1::\(\sum_{\ell=k}^{\infty} w_y(\ell)q^{-\ell} \quad \text{with } w_y(k) \neq 0\)}}
cards.anki_back: That is, the output feedback filter \(W_y(q)\) uses only outputs up to time \(t-k\) (having a delay of at least \(k\) samples).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: In terms of the predictor filter $W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]$, a predictor model is called an *output error model* (or *simulation model*) if {{c1::$W_y(q) \equiv 0$}}.
cards.raw_back: When $W_y(q) \equiv 0$ (corresponding to $H(q) \equiv 1$), the prediction $\hat{y}(t|t-1) = W_u(q)u(t) = G(q)u(t)$ is formed purely by simulating the system with the input $u(t)$ without using past measured outputs $y$.
cards.anki_front: In terms of the predictor filter \(W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]\), a predictor model is called an output error model (or simulation model) if {{c1::\(W_y(q) \equiv 0\)}}.
cards.anki_back: When \(W_y(q) \equiv 0\) (corresponding to \(H(q) \equiv 1\)), the prediction \(\hat{y}(t|t-1) = W_u(q)u(t) = G(q)u(t)\) is formed purely by simulating the system with the input \(u(t)\) without using past measured outputs \(y\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: Does Definition 4.1 (which requires the predictor filter $W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]$ to be stable) require the underlying open-loop system dynamics $G(q)$ and $H(q)$ to be stable? Illustrate with Example 4.4.
cards.raw_back:
**No!** In Example 4.4, consider the unstable ARX system $y(t) + ay(t-1) = bu(t-1) + e(t)$ with $|a| > 1$, so $G(q) = \frac{bq^{-1}}{1+aq^{-1}}$ and $H(q) = \frac{1}{1+aq^{-1}}$ are both unstable.

However, the predictor filters are $W_u(q) = H^{-1}(q)G(q) = bq^{-1}$ and $W_y(q) = 1 - H^{-1}(q) = -aq^{-1}$, which are finite impulse response (FIR) polynomials and hence **strictly stable** ($ \hat{y}(t|t-1) = -ay(t-1) + bu(t-1)$).
cards.anki_front: Does Definition 4.1 (which requires the predictor filter \(W(q) = [W_u(q) \quad W_y(q)]\) to be stable) require the underlying open-loop system dynamics \(G(q)\) and \(H(q)\) to be stable? Illustrate with Example 4.4.
cards.anki_back:
No! In Example 4.4, consider the unstable ARX system \(y(t) + ay(t-1) = bu(t-1) + e(t)\) with \(|a| > 1\), so \(G(q) = \frac{bq^{-1}}{1+aq^{-1}} \) and \(H(q) = \frac{1}{1+aq^{-1}} \) are both unstable.

However, the predictor filters are \(W_u(q) = H^{-1}(q)G(q) = bq^{-1} \) and \(W_y(q) = 1 - H^{-1}(q) = -aq^{-1} \), which are finite impulse response (FIR) polynomials and hence strictly stable ($
\hat{y}(t|t-1) = -ay(t-1) + bu(t-1)$).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
In Ljung's formal framework (Eq. 4.118), a *model set* $\mathcal{M}^*$ is defined as:
$$\mathcal{M}^* = {{c1::\{W_\alpha(q) \mid \alpha \in \mathcal{A}\}}}$$
where each $W_\alpha(q)$ is a predictor model satisfying Definition 4.1 and $\mathcal{A}$ is an index set.
cards.raw_back: A model set $\mathcal{M}^*$ is simply an unparametrized (or abstractly indexed) collection of candidate predictor models over which the search for a suitable model is conducted.
cards.anki_front:
In Ljung's formal framework (Eq. 4.118), a model set \(\mathcal{M}^*\) is defined as:

\(\mathcal{M}^* =\) {{c1::\(\{W_\alpha(q) \mid \alpha \in \mathcal{A}\} \)}}

where each \(W_\alpha(q)\) is a predictor model satisfying Definition 4.1 and \(\mathcal{A} \) is an index set.
cards.anki_back: A model set \(\mathcal{M}^*\) is simply an unparametrized (or abstractly indexed) collection of candidate predictor models over which the search for a suitable model is conducted.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
What is the model set $\mathcal{M}_n^*$ defined in Equation (4.119)?
$$\mathcal{M}_n^* = {{c1::\{\text{all predictor models such that } W_y(q) \text{ and } W_u(q) \text{ are polynomials in } q^{-1} \text{ of degree at most } n\}}}$$
cards.raw_back: This corresponds to the set of all ARX predictor models of order at most $n$.
cards.anki_front:
What is the model set \(\mathcal{M}_n^*\) defined in Equation (4.119)?

\(\mathcal{M}_n^* =\) {{c1::\(\{\text{all predictor models such that } W_y(q) \text{ and } W_u(q) \text{ are polynomials in } q^{-1} \text{ of degree at most } n\} \)}}
cards.anki_back: This corresponds to the set of all ARX predictor models of order at most \(n\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
When are two model sets $\mathcal{M}_1^*$ and $\mathcal{M}_2^*$ said to be *equal* ($\mathcal{M}_1^* = \mathcal{M}_2^*$)?
If {{c1::for every model $W_1 \in \mathcal{M}_1^*$ there exists a model $W_2 \in \mathcal{M}_2^*$ such that $W_1(e^{i\omega}) = W_2(e^{i\omega})$ for almost all $\omega$, and vice versa}}.
cards.raw_back: Equality of model sets depends only on the collection of input-output predictor frequency responses they contain, not on how they are indexed or parametrized.
cards.anki_front:
When are two model sets \(\mathcal{M}_1^*\) and \(\mathcal{M}_2^*\) said to be equal (\(\mathcal{M}_1^* = \mathcal{M}_2^*\))?
If {{c1::for every model \(W_1 \in \mathcal{M}_1^*\) there exists a model \(W_2 \in \mathcal{M}_2^*\) such that \(W_1(e^{i\omega}) = W_2(e^{i\omega})\) for almost all \(\omega\), and vice versa}}.
cards.anki_back: Equality of model sets depends only on the collection of input-output predictor frequency responses they contain, not on how they are indexed or parametrized.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
For a parametrized predictor filter $W(z, \theta) = [W_u(z, \theta) \quad W_y(z, \theta)]$ indexed by $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$, how is the $d \times 2$ predictor gradient filter matrix $\Psi(z, \theta)$ defined (Eq. 4.121a–b)?
$$\Psi(z, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}W(z, \theta) = {{c1::\left[\frac{d}{d\theta}W_u(z, \theta) \quad \frac{d}{d\theta}W_y(z, \theta)\right]}}$$
cards.raw_back: Each column $\Psi_u(z,\theta)$ and $\Psi_y(z,\theta)$ is a $d \times 1$ column vector of partial derivatives with respect to $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_d$.
cards.anki_front:
For a parametrized predictor filter \(W(z, \theta) = [W_u(z, \theta) \quad W_y(z, \theta)]\) indexed by \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d\), how is the \(d \times 2\) predictor gradient filter matrix \(\Psi(z, \theta)\) defined (Eq. 4.121a–b)?

\(\Psi(z, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}W(z, \theta) =\) {{c1::\(\left[\frac{d}{d\theta}W_u(z, \theta) \quad \frac{d}{d\theta}W_y(z, \theta)\right]\)}}
cards.anki_back: Each column \(\Psi_u(z,\theta)\) and \(\Psi_y(z,\theta)\) is a \(d \times 1\) column vector of partial derivatives with respect to \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_d\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
How is the $d \times 1$ predictor gradient signal $\psi(t, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}\hat{y}(t|\theta)$ expressed in terms of the predictor gradient filter $\Psi(q, \theta)$ and the data vector $z(t) = [u(t) \quad y(t)]^T$ (Eq. 4.121c)?
$$\psi(t, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}\hat{y}(t|\theta) = {{c1::\Psi(q, \theta)z(t)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Expanding the $d \times 2$ filter gives $\psi(t, \theta) = \Psi_u(q, \theta)u(t) + \Psi_y(q, \theta)y(t)$.
cards.anki_front:
How is the \(d \times 1\) predictor gradient signal \(\psi(t, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}\hat{y}(t|\theta)\) expressed in terms of the predictor gradient filter \(\Psi(q, \theta)\) and the data vector \(z(t) = [u(t) \quad y(t)]^T\) (Eq. 4.121c)?

\(\psi(t, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}\hat{y}(t|\theta) =\) {{c1::\(\Psi(q, \theta)z(t)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Expanding the \(d \times 2\) filter gives \(\psi(t, \theta) = \Psi_u(q, \theta)u(t) + \Psi_y(q, \theta)y(t)\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: **Definition (Model Structure $\mathcal{M}$)**: A *model structure* $\mathcal{M}$ is a {{c1::differentiable mapping from a connected subset $D_{\mathcal{M}} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ to a model set $\mathcal{M}^*$, $\mathcal{M}: D_{\mathcal{M}} \ni \theta \mapsto \mathcal{M}(\theta) = W(q, \theta) \in \mathcal{M}^*$, such that both the predictor filters $W(q, \theta)$ and the predictor gradient filters $\Psi(q, \theta)$ are stable for all $\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$}}.
cards.raw_back: Note that $\mathcal{M}$ denotes the parameter-to-model mapping itself, whereas $\mathcal{M}(\theta) = W(q,\theta)$ denotes the particular predictor model corresponding to the parameter vector $\theta$.
cards.anki_front: Definition (Model Structure \(\mathcal{M} \)): A model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) is a {{c1::differentiable mapping from a connected subset \(D_{\mathcal{M}} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) to a model set \(\mathcal{M}^*\), \(\mathcal{M}: D_{\mathcal{M}} \ni \theta \mapsto \mathcal{M}(\theta) = W(q, \theta) \in \mathcal{M}^*\), such that both the predictor filters \(W(q, \theta)\) and the predictor gradient filters \(\Psi(q, \theta)\) are stable for all \(\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \)}}.
cards.anki_back: Note that \(\mathcal{M} \) denotes the parameter-to-model mapping itself, whereas \(\mathcal{M}(\theta) = W(q,\theta)\) denotes the particular predictor model corresponding to the parameter vector \(\theta\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: In the formal definition of a model structure $\mathcal{M}: D_{\mathcal{M}} \to \mathcal{M}^*$, why do we require both openness (or that $D_{\mathcal{M}}$ is a compact subset equal to the closure of an open connected set contained in an open domain) and stability of the gradient filter $\Psi(q, \theta)$?
cards.raw_back:
1. **Openness / open neighborhood**: Ensures that the partial derivatives $\Psi(z, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}W(z, \theta)$ are unambiguously well defined at every point of $D_{\mathcal{M}}$.
2. **Compactness & Uniform Stability**: In numerical search and asymptotic convergence analysis (Chapters 7–8), restricting $\theta$ to a compact set $D_{\mathcal{M}}$ guarantees uniform exponential stability $|w_\theta(k)| \le C\bar{\lambda}^k$ ($\bar{\lambda} < 1$) across all $\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$ and ensures the minimum of the criterion is attained.
3. **Stability of $\Psi(q, \theta)$**: Gradient-based search algorithms must actually compute $\psi(t, \theta) = \Psi(q, \theta)z(t)$ from data.
cards.anki_front: In the formal definition of a model structure \(\mathcal{M}: D_{\mathcal{M}} \to \mathcal{M}^*\), why do we require both openness (or that \(D_{\mathcal{M}} \) is a compact subset equal to the closure of an open connected set contained in an open domain) and stability of the gradient filter \(\Psi(q, \theta)\)?
cards.anki_back:
1. Openness / open neighborhood: Ensures that the partial derivatives \(\Psi(z, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}W(z, \theta)\) are unambiguously well defined at every point of \(D_{\mathcal{M}} \).
2. Compactness & Uniform Stability: In numerical search and asymptotic convergence analysis (Chapters 7–8), restricting \(\theta\) to a compact set \(D_{\mathcal{M}} \) guarantees uniform exponential stability \(|w_\theta(k)| \le C\bar{\lambda}^k\) (\(\bar{\lambda} < 1\)) across all \(\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \) and ensures the minimum of the criterion is attained.
3. Stability of \(\Psi(q, \theta)\): Gradient-based search algorithms must actually compute \(\psi(t, \theta) = \Psi(q, \theta)z(t)\) from data.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
When $D_{\mathcal{M}} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ is taken to be compact, what is the uniform exponential stability bound required of the impulse responses $w_\theta(k)$ of $W(q, \theta)$ and $\Psi(q, \theta)$ across $\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$?
$$|w_\theta(k)| \le {{c1::C\bar{\lambda}^k, \qquad \bar{\lambda} < 1 \quad \forall \theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}}}}$$
cards.raw_back: Here $C < \infty$ and $\bar{\lambda} < 1$ are constants independent of $\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$, preventing poles of $W(q,\theta)$ or $\Psi(q,\theta)$ from approaching the unit circle arbitrarily closely.
cards.anki_front:
When \(D_{\mathcal{M}} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) is taken to be compact, what is the uniform exponential stability bound required of the impulse responses \(w_\theta(k)\) of \(W(q, \theta)\) and \(\Psi(q, \theta)\) across \(\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \)?

\(|w_\theta(k)| \le\) {{c1::\(C\bar{\lambda}^k, \qquad \bar{\lambda} < 1 \quad \forall \theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \)}}
cards.anki_back: Here \(C < \infty\) and \(\bar{\lambda} < 1\) are constants independent of \(\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \), preventing poles of \(W(q,\theta)\) or \(\Psi(q,\theta)\) from approaching the unit circle arbitrarily closely.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
In Example 4.5, for the ARX model $y(t) + ay(t-1) = b_1 u(t-1) + b_2 u(t-2) + e(t)$ with $\theta = [a \quad b_1 \quad b_2]^T$ and $W(q, \theta) = [b_1 q^{-1} + b_2 q^{-2} \quad -aq^{-1}]$, what is the $3 \times 2$ predictor gradient filter $\Psi(q, \theta)$?
$$\Psi(q, \theta) = {{c1::\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -q^{-1} \\ q^{-1} & 0 \\ q^{-2} & 0 \end{bmatrix}}}$$
cards.raw_back: Multiplying by $z(t) = [u(t) \quad y(t)]^T$ yields $\psi(t, \theta) = \Psi(q, \theta)z(t) = [-y(t-1) \quad u(t-1) \quad u(t-2)]^T = \varphi(t)$, which is independent of $\theta$ (linear regression).
cards.anki_front:
In Example 4.5, for the ARX model \(y(t) + ay(t-1) = b_1 u(t-1) + b_2 u(t-2) + e(t)\) with \(\theta = [a \quad b_1 \quad b_2]^T\) and \(W(q, \theta) = [b_1 q^{-1} + b_2 q^{-2} \quad -aq^{-1}]\), what is the \(3 \times 2\) predictor gradient filter \(\Psi(q, \theta)\)?

\(\Psi(q, \theta) =\) {{c1::\(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -q^{-1} \\ q^{-1} & 0 \\ q^{-2} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \)}}
cards.anki_back: Multiplying by \(z(t) = [u(t) \quad y(t)]^T\) yields \(\psi(t, \theta) = \Psi(q, \theta)z(t) = [-y(t-1) \quad u(t-1) \quad u(t-2)]^T = \varphi(t)\), which is independent of \(\theta\) (linear regression).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
For an ARMAX model $A(q)y(t) = B(q)u(t) + C(q)e(t)$ with pseudolinear regression vector $\varphi(t, \theta)$, what is the predictor gradient vector $\psi(t, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}\hat{y}(t|\theta)$?
$$\psi(t, \theta) = {{c1::\frac{1}{C(q)}\varphi(t, \theta)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Because $C(q)\hat{y}(t|\theta) = B(q)u(t) + [C(q) - A(q)]y(t) = \varphi^T(t, \theta)\theta$, differentiating with respect to $\theta$ and applying the product rule yields $C(q)\psi(t, \theta) = \varphi(t, \theta)$.
cards.anki_front:
For an ARMAX model \(A(q)y(t) = B(q)u(t) + C(q)e(t)\) with pseudolinear regression vector \(\varphi(t, \theta)\), what is the predictor gradient vector \(\psi(t, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}\hat{y}(t|\theta)\)?

\(\psi(t, \theta) =\) {{c1::\(\frac{1}{C(q)}\varphi(t, \theta)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Because \(C(q)\hat{y}(t|\theta) = B(q)u(t) + [C(q) - A(q)]y(t) = \varphi^T(t, \theta)\theta\), differentiating with respect to \(\theta\) and applying the product rule yields \(C(q)\psi(t, \theta) = \varphi(t, \theta)\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
Given $W_u(z, \theta) = H^{-1}(z, \theta)G(z, \theta)$ and $W_y(z, \theta) = 1 - H^{-1}(z, \theta)$, what are the partial derivatives $\frac{\partial W_u}{\partial \theta_i}$ and $\frac{\partial W_y}{\partial \theta_i}$ in terms of $G, H$ and their derivatives?
$$\frac{\partial W_u}{\partial \theta_i} = {{c1::H^{-1}\frac{\partial G}{\partial \theta_i} - H^{-2}G\frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta_i}}}, \qquad \frac{\partial W_y}{\partial \theta_i} = {{c1::H^{-2}\frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta_i}}}$$
cards.raw_back: Derived by applying the quotient/chain rule to $W_u = H^{-1}G$ and $W_y = 1 - H^{-1}$.
cards.anki_front:
Given \(W_u(z, \theta) = H^{-1}(z, \theta)G(z, \theta)\) and \(W_y(z, \theta) = 1 - H^{-1}(z, \theta)\), what are the partial derivatives \(\frac{\partial W_u}{\partial \theta_i} \) and \(\frac{\partial W_y}{\partial \theta_i} \) in terms of \(G, H\) and their derivatives?

\(\frac{\partial W_u}{\partial \theta_i} =\) {{c1::\(H^{-1}\frac{\partial G}{\partial \theta_i} - H^{-2}G\frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta_i} \)}} \(, \qquad \frac{\partial W_y}{\partial \theta_i} =\) {{c1::\(H^{-2}\frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta_i} \)}}
cards.anki_back: Derived by applying the quotient/chain rule to \(W_u = H^{-1}G\) and \(W_y = 1 - H^{-1} \).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
How is the $d \times 2$ predictor gradient filter $\Psi(q, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}W(q, \theta)$ factored in terms of $T'(q, \theta) = \left[\frac{d}{d\theta}G(q, \theta) \quad \frac{d}{d\theta}H(q, \theta)\right]$ (Eq. 4.124–4.125)?
$$\Psi(q, \theta) = {{c1::\frac{1}{(H(q, \theta))^2} T'(q, \theta) \begin{bmatrix} H(q, \theta) & 0 \\ -G(q, \theta) & 1 \end{bmatrix}}}$$
cards.raw_back: Equivalently written as $H^{-1}(q, \theta)T'(q, \theta)\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -H^{-1}(q, \theta)G(q, \theta) & H^{-1}(q, \theta) \end{bmatrix}$. Thus differentiability and stability of $W$ are assured by differentiability of $T$ and stability of $G, H, H^{-1}$.
cards.anki_front:
How is the \(d \times 2\) predictor gradient filter \(\Psi(q, \theta) = \frac{d}{d\theta}W(q, \theta)\) factored in terms of \(T'(q, \theta) = \left[\frac{d}{d\theta}G(q, \theta) \quad \frac{d}{d\theta}H(q, \theta)\right]\) (Eq. 4.124–4.125)?

\(\Psi(q, \theta) =\) {{c1::\(\frac{1}{(H(q, \theta))^2} T'(q, \theta) \begin{bmatrix} H(q, \theta) & 0 \\ -G(q, \theta) & 1 \end{bmatrix} \)}}
cards.anki_back: Equivalently written as \(H^{-1}(q, \theta)T'(q, \theta)\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -H^{-1}(q, \theta)G(q, \theta) & H^{-1}(q, \theta) \end{bmatrix} \). Thus differentiability and stability of \(W\) are assured by differentiability of \(T\) and stability of \(G, H, H^{-1} \).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
**Lemma 4.1 (Transfer-Function Model Structure)**: The general SISO polynomial family $A(q)y(t) = \frac{B(q)}{F(q)}u(t) + \frac{C(q)}{D(q)}e(t)$ defines a valid model structure $\mathcal{M}$ when $\theta$ is confined to:
$$D_{\mathcal{M}} = {{c1::\{\theta \mid F(z)\cdot C(z) \text{ has no zeros on or outside the unit circle } |z| \ge 1\}}}$$
cards.raw_back: When $D_{\mathcal{M}}$ is required to be compact with uniform stability, the roots of $F(z)$ and $C(z)$ are restricted to lie strictly inside a circle of radius $1 - \epsilon$ ($\epsilon > 0$). Notice that the roots of $A(z)$ and $D(z)$ do NOT need to lie inside the unit circle for the predictor and its gradients to be stable!
cards.anki_front:
Lemma 4.1 (Transfer-Function Model Structure): The general SISO polynomial family \(A(q)y(t) = \frac{B(q)}{F(q)}u(t) + \frac{C(q)}{D(q)}e(t)\) defines a valid model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) when \(\theta\) is confined to:

\(D_{\mathcal{M}} =\) {{c1::\(\{\theta \mid F(z)\cdot C(z) \text{ has no zeros on or outside the unit circle } |z| \ge 1\} \)}}
cards.anki_back: When \(D_{\mathcal{M}} \) is required to be compact with uniform stability, the roots of \(F(z)\) and \(C(z)\) are restricted to lie strictly inside a circle of radius \(1 - \epsilon\) (\(\epsilon > 0\)). Notice that the roots of \(A(z)\) and \(D(z)\) do NOT need to lie inside the unit circle for the predictor and its gradients to be stable!

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: How is Lemma 4.1 proved for the general transfer-function model $A(q)y(t) = \frac{B(q)}{F(q)}u(t) + \frac{C(q)}{D(q)}e(t)$?
cards.raw_back:
The predictor filters are:
$$W_u(z, \theta) = \frac{B(z)D(z)}{C(z)F(z)} \quad \text{and} \quad W_y(z, \theta) = 1 - \frac{D(z)A(z)}{C(z)}$$
Their partial derivatives with respect to the polynomial coefficients in $\theta$, such as:
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial c_k}W_u(z, \theta) = -\frac{B(z)D(z)z^{-k}}{[C(z)]^2 F(z)}$$
have denominators involving only powers of $C(z)$ and $F(z)$. Hence $W_u, W_y$ and all their $\theta$-gradients are analytic in $|z| \ge 1$ (stable) whenever $F(z)\cdot C(z) \neq 0$ for $|z| \ge 1$.
cards.anki_front: How is Lemma 4.1 proved for the general transfer-function model \(A(q)y(t) = \frac{B(q)}{F(q)}u(t) + \frac{C(q)}{D(q)}e(t)\)?
cards.anki_back:
The predictor filters are:
\[W_u(z, \theta) = \frac{B(z)D(z)}{C(z)F(z)} \quad \text{and} \quad W_y(z, \theta) = 1 - \frac{D(z)A(z)}{C(z)} \]
Their partial derivatives with respect to the polynomial coefficients in \(\theta\), such as:
\[\frac{\partial}{\partial c_k}W_u(z, \theta) = -\frac{B(z)D(z)z^{-k}}{[C(z)]^2 F(z)} \]
have denominators involving only powers of \(C(z)\) and \(F(z)\). Hence \(W_u, W_y\) and all their \(\theta\)-gradients are analytic in \(|z| \ge 1\) (stable) whenever \(F(z)\cdot C(z) \neq 0\) for \(|z| \ge 1\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
**Lemma 4.2 (State-Space Model Structure)**: Consider the innovations state-space parametrization $x(t+1) = A(\theta)x(t) + B(\theta)u(t) + K(\theta)e(t)$, $y(t) = C(\theta)x(t) + e(t)$ with differentiable matrices $A(\theta), B(\theta), K(\theta), C(\theta)$. It forms a valid model structure on:
$$D_{\mathcal{M}} = {{c1::\{\theta \mid \text{all eigenvalues of } A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta) \text{ are strictly inside the unit circle}\}}}$$
cards.raw_back: Because $A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta)$ is the state transition matrix of the one-step-ahead predictor $\hat{x}(t+1|\theta) = [A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta)]\hat{x}(t|\theta) + B(\theta)u(t) + K(\theta)y(t)$, its eigenvalues govern the stability of both $W(q,\theta)$ and $\Psi(q,\theta)$.
cards.anki_front:
Lemma 4.2 (State-Space Model Structure): Consider the innovations state-space parametrization \(x(t+1) = A(\theta)x(t) + B(\theta)u(t) + K(\theta)e(t)\), \(y(t) = C(\theta)x(t) + e(t)\) with differentiable matrices \(A(\theta), B(\theta), K(\theta), C(\theta)\). It forms a valid model structure on:

\(D_{\mathcal{M}} =\) {{c1::\(\{\theta \mid \text{all eigenvalues of } A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta) \text{ are strictly inside the unit circle}\} \)}}
cards.anki_back: Because \(A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta)\) is the state transition matrix of the one-step-ahead predictor \(\hat{x}(t+1|\theta) = [A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta)]\hat{x}(t|\theta) + B(\theta)u(t) + K(\theta)y(t)\), its eigenvalues govern the stability of both \(W(q,\theta)\) and \(\Psi(q,\theta)\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
When the Kalman gain $K(\theta)$ in a state-space model is computed from the steady-state Riccati equation (4.87) using noise covariance matrices $R_1(\theta), R_2(\theta), R_{12}(\theta)$ (with $R_{12}=0, R_2 > 0$), what standard Kalman filter conditions on $(A(\theta), R_1(\theta), C(\theta))$ guarantee that $A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta)$ has all eigenvalues inside the unit circle (Eq. 4.126)?
$$D_{\mathcal{M}} = {{c1::\{\theta \mid [A(\theta), R_1^{1/2}(\theta)] \text{ is stabilizable and } [A(\theta), C(\theta)] \text{ is detectable}\}}}$$
cards.raw_back: By standard Kalman filter theory (Anderson & Moore, 1979), stabilizability of $[A(\theta), R_1(\theta)]$ and detectability of $[A(\theta), C(\theta)]$ guarantee a unique positive semidefinite Riccati solution $P(\theta)$ that is differentiable in $\theta$ and yields an asymptotically stable predictor matrix $A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta)$.
cards.anki_front:
When the Kalman gain \(K(\theta)\) in a state-space model is computed from the steady-state Riccati equation (4.87) using noise covariance matrices \(R_1(\theta), R_2(\theta), R_{12}(\theta)\) (with \(R_{12}=0, R_2 > 0\)), what standard Kalman filter conditions on \((A(\theta), R_1(\theta), C(\theta))\) guarantee that \(A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta)\) has all eigenvalues inside the unit circle (Eq. 4.126)?

\(D_{\mathcal{M}} =\) {{c1::\(\{\theta \mid [A(\theta), R_1^{1/2}(\theta)] \text{ is stabilizable and } [A(\theta), C(\theta)] \text{ is detectable}\} \)}}
cards.anki_back: By standard Kalman filter theory (Anderson & Moore, 1979), stabilizability of \([A(\theta), R_1(\theta)]\) and detectability of \([A(\theta), C(\theta)]\) guarantee a unique positive semidefinite Riccati solution \(P(\theta)\) that is differentiable in \(\theta\) and yields an asymptotically stable predictor matrix \(A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta)\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: **Definition 4.4 (Containment of Model Structures)**: A model structure $\mathcal{M}_1$ is said to be *contained in* $\mathcal{M}_2$, written $\mathcal{M}_1 \subset \mathcal{M}_2$ (Eq. 4.127), if {{c1::$D_{\mathcal{M}_1} \subset D_{\mathcal{M}_2}$ and the mapping $\mathcal{M}_1$ is obtained by restricting $\mathcal{M}_2$ to $\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}_1}$}}.
cards.raw_back: The archetypical situation is hierarchical model order nesting: $\mathcal{M}_2$ defines $n$th-order models and $\mathcal{M}_1$ defines $m$th-order models ($m < n$) obtained by fixing the trailing parameters to zero.
cards.anki_front: Definition 4.4 (Containment of Model Structures): A model structure \(\mathcal{M}_1\) is said to be contained in \(\mathcal{M}_2\), written \(\mathcal{M}_1 \subset \mathcal{M}_2\) (Eq. 4.127), if {{c1::\(D_{\mathcal{M}_1} \subset D_{\mathcal{M}_2} \) and the mapping \(\mathcal{M}_1\) is obtained by restricting \(\mathcal{M}_2\) to \(\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}_1} \)}}.
cards.anki_back: The archetypical situation is hierarchical model order nesting: \(\mathcal{M}_2\) defines \(n\)th-order models and \(\mathcal{M}_1\) defines \(m\)th-order models (\(m < n\)) obtained by fixing the trailing parameters to zero.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
**Definition 4.5 (Independently Parametrized Transfer Function and Noise Model)**: A model structure $\mathcal{M}$ has an *independently parametrized transfer function and noise model* (Eq. 4.128) if:
$$\theta = \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ \eta \end{bmatrix}, \quad D_{\mathcal{M}} = {{c1::D_\rho \times D_\eta}}, \quad T(q, \theta) = {{c1::[G(q, \rho) \quad H(q, \eta)]}}$$
cards.raw_back: Here $G$ depends only on $\rho \in D_\rho$ and $H$ depends only on $\eta \in D_\eta$, with no shared parameters between the plant dynamics and the noise model.
cards.anki_front:
Definition 4.5 (Independently Parametrized Transfer Function and Noise Model): A model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) has an independently parametrized transfer function and noise model (Eq. 4.128) if:

\(\theta = \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ \eta \end{bmatrix}, \quad D_{\mathcal{M}} =\) {{c1::\(D_\rho \times D_\eta\)}} \(, \quad T(q, \theta) =\) {{c1::\([G(q, \rho) \quad H(q, \eta)]\)}}
cards.anki_back: Here \(G\) depends only on \(\rho \in D_\rho\) and \(H\) depends only on \(\eta \in D_\eta\), with no shared parameters between the plant dynamics and the noise model.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
Within the general SISO polynomial family $A(q)y(t) = \frac{B(q)}{F(q)}u(t) + \frac{C(q)}{D(q)}e(t)$, which special cases correspond to an *independently parametrized transfer function and noise model* (Definition 4.5)?
The cases with {{c1::$A(q) \equiv 1$ (such as the Box-Jenkins and Output-Error structures)}}.
cards.raw_back: When $A(q) \equiv 1$, $G(q, \rho) = \frac{B(q)}{F(q)}$ and $H(q, \eta) = \frac{C(q)}{D(q)}$ share no common polynomial $A(q)$.
cards.anki_front:
Within the general SISO polynomial family \(A(q)y(t) = \frac{B(q)}{F(q)}u(t) + \frac{C(q)}{D(q)}e(t)\), which special cases correspond to an independently parametrized transfer function and noise model (Definition 4.5)?
The cases with {{c1::\(A(q) \equiv 1\) (such as the Box-Jenkins and Output-Error structures)}}.
cards.anki_back: When \(A(q) \equiv 1\), \(G(q, \rho) = \frac{B(q)}{F(q)} \) and \(H(q, \eta) = \frac{C(q)}{D(q)} \) share no common polynomial \(A(q)\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: If a candidate model set $\mathcal{M}^* = \{W_1(q), W_2(q), W_3(q)\}$ is finite and indexed by a parameter $\theta$ ranging over a finite set of points, does this qualify as a 'model structure' under Definition 4.3? Do the estimation and convergence results of Chapters 7 and 8 still apply?
cards.raw_back:
1. **Not a formal model structure**: Because $\theta$ ranges over discrete isolated points rather than an open/connected subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$, differentiability with respect to $\theta$ (Definition 4.3) does not apply.
2. **Estimation and convergence still hold**: The prediction-error estimation procedures (Sections 7.1–7.4) and convergence analysis (Sections 8.1–8.5) still make complete sense for finite model sets.
cards.anki_front: If a candidate model set \(\mathcal{M}^* = \{W_1(q), W_2(q), W_3(q)\} \) is finite and indexed by a parameter \(\theta\) ranging over a finite set of points, does this qualify as a 'model structure' under Definition 4.3? Do the estimation and convergence results of Chapters 7 and 8 still apply?
cards.anki_back:
1. Not a formal model structure: Because \(\theta\) ranges over discrete isolated points rather than an open/connected subset of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), differentiability with respect to \(\theta\) (Definition 4.3) does not apply.
2. Estimation and convergence still hold: The prediction-error estimation procedures (Sections 7.1–7.4) and convergence analysis (Sections 8.1–8.5) still make complete sense for finite model sets.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
How is the *range* $\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})$ of a model structure $\mathcal{M}: D_{\mathcal{M}} \to \mathcal{M}^*$ defined, and how does it generate a model set?
$$\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}) = \text{Range } \mathcal{M} = {{c1::\{\mathcal{M}(\theta) \mid \theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}}\}}}$$
cards.raw_back: The range $\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}) \subset \mathcal{M}^*$ is the subset of predictor models in $\mathcal{M}^*$ reachable as $\theta$ varies over $D_{\mathcal{M}}$. Finding a model structure $\mathcal{M}$ whose range equals a desired model set $\mathcal{M}^*$ is a central problem in system identification.
cards.anki_front:
How is the range \(\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})\) of a model structure \(\mathcal{M}: D_{\mathcal{M}} \to \mathcal{M}^*\) defined, and how does it generate a model set?

\(\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}) = \text{Range } \mathcal{M} =\) {{c1::\(\{\mathcal{M}(\theta) \mid \theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}}\} \)}}
cards.anki_back: The range \(\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}) \subset \mathcal{M}^*\) is the subset of predictor models in \(\mathcal{M}^*\) reachable as \(\theta\) varies over \(D_{\mathcal{M}} \). Finding a model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) whose range equals a desired model set \(\mathcal{M}^*\) is a central problem in system identification.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
In Example 4.6, how do we construct a model structure $\mathcal{M}$ whose range $\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})$ equals the 3rd-order ARX model set $\mathcal{M}_3^*$ (all models where $W_y(q), W_u(q)$ are polynomials in $q^{-1}$ of degree $\le 3$)?
Take $D_{\mathcal{M}} = \mathbb{R}^6$, $\theta = [a_1 \; a_2 \; a_3 \; b_1 \; b_2 \; b_3]^T$, and:
$$W_y(q, \theta) = {{c1::-a_1 q^{-1} - a_2 q^{-2} - a_3 q^{-3}}}, \qquad W_u(q, \theta) = {{c1::b_1 q^{-1} + b_2 q^{-2} + b_3 q^{-3}}}$$
cards.raw_back: Every pair of polynomials in $q^{-1}$ of degree at most 3 is uniquely represented by a point $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^6$, so $\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}) = \mathcal{M}_3^*$.
cards.anki_front:
In Example 4.6, how do we construct a model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) whose range \(\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})\) equals the 3rd-order ARX model set \(\mathcal{M}_3^*\) (all models where \(W_y(q), W_u(q)\) are polynomials in \(q^{-1} \) of degree \(\le 3\))?
Take \(D_{\mathcal{M}} = \mathbb{R}^6\), \(\theta = [a_1 \; a_2 \; a_3 \; b_1 \; b_2 \; b_3]^T\), and:

\(W_y(q, \theta) =\) {{c1::\(-a_1 q^{-1} - a_2 q^{-2} - a_3 q^{-3} \)}} \(, \qquad W_u(q, \theta) =\) {{c1::\(b_1 q^{-1} + b_2 q^{-2} + b_3 q^{-3} \)}}
cards.anki_back: Every pair of polynomials in \(q^{-1} \) of degree at most 3 is uniquely represented by a point \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}^6\), so \(\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}) = \mathcal{M}_3^*\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
When a desired model set $\mathcal{M}^*$ cannot be represented as the range of a single model structure with good identifiability properties, how is $\mathcal{M}^*$ represented using multiple model structures $\{\mathcal{M}_i\}_{i=1}^\beta$ (Eq. 4.129)?
$$\mathcal{M}^* = {{c1::\bigcup_{i=1}^{\beta} \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}_i)}}$$
cards.raw_back: The model set $\mathcal{M}^*$ is covered as a union of ranges of several model structures $\mathcal{M}_i$.
cards.anki_front:
When a desired model set \(\mathcal{M}^*\) cannot be represented as the range of a single model structure with good identifiability properties, how is \(\mathcal{M}^*\) represented using multiple model structures \(\{\mathcal{M}_i\}_{i=1}^\beta\) (Eq. 4.129)?

\(\mathcal{M}^* =\) {{c1::\(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\beta} \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}_i)\)}}
cards.anki_back: The model set \(\mathcal{M}^*\) is covered as a union of ranges of several model structures \(\mathcal{M}_i\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: What is the differential-geometric analogy between a model set $\mathcal{M}^*$, a model structure $\mathcal{M}_i: D_{\mathcal{M}_i} \to \mathcal{M}^*$, and the union representation $\mathcal{M}^* = \bigcup_{i=1}^\beta \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}_i)$ (Eq. 4.129)? Where is this essential in system identification?
cards.raw_back:
1. **Geometric analogy**: The model set $\mathcal{M}^*$ is analogous to a smooth **manifold**, while each model structure $\mathcal{M}_i: D_{\mathcal{M}_i} \subset \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}_i) \subset \mathcal{M}^*$ acts as a local **coordinate chart** (atlas) parametrizing a patch of the manifold.
2. **Where essential**: Multi-output (MIMO) linear state-space systems of a given McMillan degree $n$ cannot be globally smoothly parametrized by a single canonical form without singularities; they require an atlas of overlapping canonical parametrizations $\mathcal{M}_i$ (Appendix 4A). It is also used when searching across models of different orders.
cards.anki_front: What is the differential-geometric analogy between a model set \(\mathcal{M}^*\), a model structure \(\mathcal{M}_i: D_{\mathcal{M}_i} \to \mathcal{M}^*\), and the union representation \(\mathcal{M}^* = \bigcup_{i=1}^\beta \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}_i)\) (Eq. 4.129)? Where is this essential in system identification?
cards.anki_back:
1. Geometric analogy: The model set \(\mathcal{M}^*\) is analogous to a smooth manifold, while each model structure \(\mathcal{M}_i: D_{\mathcal{M}_i} \subset \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M}_i) \subset \mathcal{M}^*\) acts as a local coordinate chart (atlas) parametrizing a patch of the manifold.
2. Where essential: Multi-output (MIMO) linear state-space systems of a given McMillan degree \(n\) cannot be globally smoothly parametrized by a single canonical form without singularities; they require an atlas of overlapping canonical parametrizations \(\mathcal{M}_i\) (Appendix 4A). It is also used when searching across models of different orders.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: According to Ljung (Section 4.5, 'Identifiability Properties'), what are the **two distinct legs** of the identifiability problem in system identification?
cards.raw_back:
1. **Experimental data informativity** (Sections 8.2–8.3): Whether the experimental input-output data set is informative enough to distinguish between *non-equal* models ($W_1(e^{i\omega}) \neq W_2(e^{i\omega})$).
2. **Model structure injectivity / invertibility** (Section 4.5–4.6): Assuming the data can distinguish non-equal models, whether different parameter values $\theta \neq \theta^*$ in $D_{\mathcal{M}}$ can produce *equal* predictor models $\mathcal{M}(\theta) = \mathcal{M}(\theta^*)$ (i.e., whether the mapping $\mathcal{M}$ is injective).
cards.anki_front: According to Ljung (Section 4.5, 'Identifiability Properties'), what are the two distinct legs of the identifiability problem in system identification?
cards.anki_back:
1. Experimental data informativity (Sections 8.2–8.3): Whether the experimental input-output data set is informative enough to distinguish between non-equal models (\(W_1(e^{i\omega}) \neq W_2(e^{i\omega})\)).
2. Model structure injectivity / invertibility (Section 4.5–4.6): Assuming the data can distinguish non-equal models, whether different parameter values \(\theta \neq \theta^*\) in \(D_{\mathcal{M}} \) can produce equal predictor models \(\mathcal{M}(\theta) = \mathcal{M}(\theta^*)\) (i.e., whether the mapping \(\mathcal{M} \) is injective).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
**Definition 4.6 (Global Identifiability at a Point $\theta^*$)**: A model structure $\mathcal{M}$ is *globally identifiable at $\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$* (Eq. 4.130) if:
$${{c1::\mathcal{M}(\theta) = \mathcal{M}(\theta^*), \quad \theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \implies \theta = \theta^*}}$$
cards.raw_back: In terms of the transfer functions, $W(e^{i\omega}, \theta) = W(e^{i\omega}, \theta^*)$ for almost all $\omega$ (or $G(z,\theta) \equiv G(z,\theta^*)$ and $H(z,\theta) \equiv H(z,\theta^*)$) for $\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$ implies $\theta = \theta^*$.
cards.anki_front:
Definition 4.6 (Global Identifiability at a Point \(\theta^*\)): A model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) is globally identifiable at \(\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \) (Eq. 4.130) if:
{{c1::\(\mathcal{M}(\theta) = \mathcal{M}(\theta^*), \quad \theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \implies \theta = \theta^*\)}}
cards.anki_back: In terms of the transfer functions, \(W(e^{i\omega}, \theta) = W(e^{i\omega}, \theta^*)\) for almost all \(\omega\) (or \(G(z,\theta) \equiv G(z,\theta^*)\) and \(H(z,\theta) \equiv H(z,\theta^*)\)) for \(\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \) implies \(\theta = \theta^*\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: **Definition 4.7 (Strict Global Identifiability)**: A model structure $\mathcal{M}$ is *strictly globally identifiable* if {{c1::it is globally identifiable at **all** $\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$}}.
cards.raw_back: That is, the mapping $\mathcal{M}: D_{\mathcal{M}} \to \mathcal{M}^*$ is strictly one-to-one (injective) everywhere on $D_{\mathcal{M}}$ without any exceptional points.
cards.anki_front: Definition 4.7 (Strict Global Identifiability): A model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) is strictly globally identifiable if {{c1::it is globally identifiable at all \(\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \)}}.
cards.anki_back: That is, the mapping \(\mathcal{M}: D_{\mathcal{M}} \to \mathcal{M}^*\) is strictly one-to-one (injective) everywhere on \(D_{\mathcal{M}} \) without any exceptional points.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: **Definition 4.8 (Global Identifiability of a Model Structure)**: A model structure $\mathcal{M}$ is *globally identifiable* if {{c1::it is globally identifiable at **almost all** $\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$}}.
cards.raw_back: Specifically, $\mathcal{M}$ is globally identifiable at all $\theta^* \in \tilde{D}_{\mathcal{M}} \subset D_{\mathcal{M}}$, where the exceptional set $\delta D_{\mathcal{M}} = \{\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \mid \theta \notin \tilde{D}_{\mathcal{M}}\}$ is a set of Lebesgue measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^d$ (typically a union of lower-dimensional hypersurfaces).
cards.anki_front: Definition 4.8 (Global Identifiability of a Model Structure): A model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) is globally identifiable if {{c1::it is globally identifiable at almost all \(\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \)}}.
cards.anki_back: Specifically, \(\mathcal{M} \) is globally identifiable at all \(\theta^* \in \tilde{D}_{\mathcal{M}} \subset D_{\mathcal{M}} \), where the exceptional set \(\delta D_{\mathcal{M}} = \{\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \mid \theta \notin \tilde{D}_{\mathcal{M}}\} \) is a set of Lebesgue measure zero in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (typically a union of lower-dimensional hypersurfaces).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: Why does Definition 4.8 allow an exceptional set $\delta D_{\mathcal{M}}$ of Lebesgue measure zero (where global identifiability fails) instead of demanding *strict* global identifiability (Definition 4.7) everywhere on $D_{\mathcal{M}}$?
cards.raw_back: Because in standard linear transfer-function structures (such as ARMAX, Box-Jenkins, or higher-order ARX models with common factors), global identifiability is inevitably lost on **lower-dimensional hypersurfaces** $\delta D_{\mathcal{M}} \subset D_{\mathcal{M}}$ corresponding to **lower-order systems** (where pole-zero cancellations occur or leading/coupling coefficients vanish). Requiring strict global identifiability everywhere would rule out almost all standard rational transfer-function model structures!
cards.anki_front: Why does Definition 4.8 allow an exceptional set \(\delta D_{\mathcal{M}} \) of Lebesgue measure zero (where global identifiability fails) instead of demanding strict global identifiability (Definition 4.7) everywhere on \(D_{\mathcal{M}} \)?
cards.anki_back: Because in standard linear transfer-function structures (such as ARMAX, Box-Jenkins, or higher-order ARX models with common factors), global identifiability is inevitably lost on lower-dimensional hypersurfaces \(\delta D_{\mathcal{M}} \subset D_{\mathcal{M}} \) corresponding to lower-order systems (where pole-zero cancellations occur or leading/coupling coefficients vanish). Requiring strict global identifiability everywhere would rule out almost all standard rational transfer-function model structures!

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front: Consider a first-order ARX model $y(t) + ay(t-1) = bu(t-1) + e(t)$ versus a second-order model when $b=0$ (or with a common factor $(1 + f q^{-1})$). How does this illustrate the exceptional hypersurface $\delta D_{\mathcal{M}}$ where global identifiability fails?
cards.raw_back:
- In the first-order ARX structure $W_u(q,\theta) = bq^{-1}, W_y(q,\theta) = -aq^{-1}$, $\mathcal{M}$ is **strictly globally identifiable** for all $\theta = [a \; b]^T \in \mathbb{R}^2$.
- However, in an OE structure $y(t) = \frac{b q^{-1}}{1 + f q^{-1}}u(t) + e(t)$ or a 2nd-order ARMAX/ARX structure with a pole-zero pair, whenever $b = 0$ (input disconnects from output, $G(q,\theta) \equiv 0$), the pole parameter $f$ disappears from $W(q,\theta)$ completely. Thus the line $\delta D_{\mathcal{M}} = \{[b \; f]^T \mid b = 0\}$ is a 1D hypersurface of measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^2$ where global identifiability fails.
cards.anki_front: Consider a first-order ARX model \(y(t) + ay(t-1) = bu(t-1) + e(t)\) versus a second-order model when \(b=0\) (or with a common factor \((1 + f q^{-1})\)). How does this illustrate the exceptional hypersurface \(\delta D_{\mathcal{M}} \) where global identifiability fails?
cards.anki_back:
- In the first-order ARX structure \(W_u(q,\theta) = bq^{-1}, W_y(q,\theta) = -aq^{-1} \), \(\mathcal{M} \) is strictly globally identifiable for all \(\theta = [a \; b]^T \in \mathbb{R}^2\).
- However, in an OE structure \(y(t) = \frac{b q^{-1}}{1 + f q^{-1}}u(t) + e(t)\) or a 2nd-order ARMAX/ARX structure with a pole-zero pair, whenever \(b = 0\) (input disconnects from output, \(G(q,\theta) \equiv 0\)), the pole parameter \(f\) disappears from \(W(q,\theta)\) completely. Thus the line \(\delta D_{\mathcal{M}} = \{[b \; f]^T \mid b = 0\} \) is a 1D hypersurface of measure zero in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) where global identifiability fails.

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
How is *local identifiability* of a model structure $\mathcal{M}$ at a point $\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$ defined (Eq. 4.131)?
There exists an $\varepsilon > 0$ such that:
$${{c1::\mathcal{M}(\theta) = \mathcal{M}(\theta^*), \quad \theta \in \mathcal{B}(\theta^*, \varepsilon) \implies \theta = \theta^*}}$$
where $\mathcal{B}(\theta^*, \varepsilon) = \{\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \mid \|\theta - \theta^*\| < \varepsilon\}$ is an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of $\theta^*$.
cards.raw_back: (Strict) local identifiability of the whole model structure $\mathcal{M}$ is defined analogously to Definitions 4.7 and 4.8 (for all $\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$, or for almost all $\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$).
cards.anki_front:
How is local identifiability of a model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) at a point \(\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \) defined (Eq. 4.131)?
There exists an \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that:
{{c1::\(\mathcal{M}(\theta) = \mathcal{M}(\theta^*), \quad \theta \in \mathcal{B}(\theta^*, \varepsilon) \implies \theta = \theta^*\)}}
where \(\mathcal{B}(\theta^*, \varepsilon) = \{\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \mid \|\theta - \theta^*\| < \varepsilon\} \) is an \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood of \(\theta^*\).
cards.anki_back: (Strict) local identifiability of the whole model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) is defined analogously to Definitions 4.7 and 4.8 (for all \(\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \), or for almost all \(\theta^* \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \)).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
Given a true/ideal system description $\mathcal{S}: y(t) = G_0(q)u(t) + H_0(q)e(t)$ (Eq. 4.132), when do we say that the true system is in the model set ($\mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{M}^*$ or $\mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})$)?
When {{c1::there exists at least one parameter vector $\theta_0 \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$ such that $\mathcal{M}(\theta_0) = \mathcal{S}$ (i.e., $G(e^{i\omega}, \theta_0) = G_0(e^{i\omega})$ and $H(e^{i\omega}, \theta_0) = H_0(e^{i\omega})$ for almost all $\omega$)}}.
cards.raw_back: With slight abuse of notation, Ljung writes $\mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{M}$ to mean $\mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})$.
cards.anki_front:
Given a true/ideal system description \(\mathcal{S}: y(t) = G_0(q)u(t) + H_0(q)e(t)\) (Eq. 4.132), when do we say that the true system is in the model set (\(\mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{M}^*\) or \(\mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})\))?
When {{c1::there exists at least one parameter vector \(\theta_0 \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \) such that \(\mathcal{M}(\theta_0) = \mathcal{S} \) (i.e., \(G(e^{i\omega}, \theta_0) = G_0(e^{i\omega})\) and \(H(e^{i\omega}, \theta_0) = H_0(e^{i\omega})\) for almost all \(\omega\))}}.
cards.anki_back: With slight abuse of notation, Ljung writes \(\mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{M} \) to mean \(\mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
For a system description $\mathcal{S}: y(t) = G_0(q)u(t) + H_0(q)e(t)$ and a model structure $\mathcal{M}$ (Eq. 4.133), how is the set of true parameter vectors $D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M})$ defined (Eq. 4.134)?
$$D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) = {{c1::\{\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \mid G_0(z) = G(z, \theta), \; H_0(z) = H(z, \theta) \text{ for almost all } z\}}}$$
cards.raw_back: Equivalently, $D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) = \{\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \mid \mathcal{M}(\theta) = \mathcal{S}\}$ is the preimage $\mathcal{M}^{-1}(\{\mathcal{S}\})$ of the system $\mathcal{S}$ under the model structure mapping $\mathcal{M}$.
cards.anki_front:
For a system description \(\mathcal{S}: y(t) = G_0(q)u(t) + H_0(q)e(t)\) and a model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) (Eq. 4.133), how is the set of true parameter vectors \(D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M})\) defined (Eq. 4.134)?

\(D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) =\) {{c1::\(\{\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \mid G_0(z) = G(z, \theta), \; H_0(z) = H(z, \theta) \text{ for almost all } z\} \)}}
cards.anki_back: Equivalently, \(D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) = \{\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \mid \mathcal{M}(\theta) = \mathcal{S}\} \) is the preimage \(\mathcal{M}^{-1}(\{\mathcal{S}\})\) of the system \(\mathcal{S} \) under the model structure mapping \(\mathcal{M} \).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
Suppose the true system $\mathcal{S}$ belongs to the range of $\mathcal{M}$ with $\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{M}(\theta_0)$, and suppose $\mathcal{M}$ is *globally identifiable at $\theta_0$*. What is the set of true parameter vectors $D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M})$ (Eq. 4.135)?
$$D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) = {{c1::\{\theta_0\}}}$$
cards.raw_back: It reduces to a singleton containing only the unique true parameter vector $\theta_0$.
cards.anki_front:
Suppose the true system \(\mathcal{S} \) belongs to the range of \(\mathcal{M} \) with \(\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{M}(\theta_0)\), and suppose \(\mathcal{M} \) is globally identifiable at \(\theta_0\). What is the set of true parameter vectors \(D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M})\) (Eq. 4.135)?

\(D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) =\) {{c1::\(\{\theta_0\} \)}}
cards.anki_back: It reduces to a singleton containing only the unique true parameter vector \(\theta_0\).

cards.subdeck: 4.5 Model Sets, Model Structures, and Identifiability - Some Formal Aspects
cards.raw_front:
What happens to the set of true parameter vectors $D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) = \{\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \mid \mathcal{M}(\theta) = \mathcal{S}\}$ in each of the following three scenarios?
1. $\mathcal{S} \notin \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})$ (undermodeling)
2. $\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{M}(\theta_0)$ and $\mathcal{M}$ is globally identifiable at $\theta_0$
3. $\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{M}(\theta_0)$ but $\theta_0 \in \delta D_{\mathcal{M}}$ (over-parametrization / unidentifiable at $\theta_0$)
cards.raw_back:
1. **Undermodeling ($\mathcal{S} \notin \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})$)**: $D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) = \emptyset$ (the empty set).
2. **Globally identifiable at $\theta_0$**: $D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) = \{\theta_0\}$ (a singleton).
3. **Over-parametrized / unidentifiable at $\theta_0 \in \delta D_{\mathcal{M}}$**: $D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M})$ is a non-singleton set (typically a continuum/submanifold of equivalent parameter vectors that all yield the exact same input-output predictor as $\mathcal{S}$, e.g., arbitrary cancelling pole-zero pairs).
cards.anki_front:
What happens to the set of true parameter vectors \(D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) = \{\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \mid \mathcal{M}(\theta) = \mathcal{S}\} \) in each of the following three scenarios?
1. \(\mathcal{S} \notin \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})\) (undermodeling)
2. \(\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{M}(\theta_0)\) and \(\mathcal{M} \) is globally identifiable at \(\theta_0\)
3. \(\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{M}(\theta_0)\) but \(\theta_0 \in \delta D_{\mathcal{M}} \) (over-parametrization / unidentifiable at \(\theta_0\))
cards.anki_back:
1. Undermodeling (\(\mathcal{S} \notin \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{M})\)): \(D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) = \emptyset\) (the empty set).
2. Globally identifiable at \(\theta_0\): \(D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M}) = \{\theta_0\} \) (a singleton).
3. Over-parametrized / unidentifiable at \(\theta_0 \in \delta D_{\mathcal{M}} \): \(D_T(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{M})\) is a non-singleton set (typically a continuum/submanifold of equivalent parameter vectors that all yield the exact same input-output predictor as \(\mathcal{S} \), e.g., arbitrary cancelling pole-zero pairs).

cards.raw_front: According to Definition 4.6 and (4.116), what is the necessary and sufficient transfer-function condition (4.136) for an LTI model structure $\mathcal{M}$ to be **globally identifiable at $\theta^*$**?
cards.raw_back:
$$G(z, \theta) \equiv G(z, \theta^*) \quad \text{and} \quad H(z, \theta) \equiv H(z, \theta^*) \quad \text{for almost all } z \implies \theta = \theta^* \qquad (4.136)$$

That is, no other parameter vector $\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$ can produce the exact same input-output transfer function $G(z,\theta)$ and noise transfer function $H(z,\theta)$ almost everywhere on the complex $z$-plane.
cards.anki_front: According to Definition 4.6 and (4.116), what is the necessary and sufficient transfer-function condition (4.136) for an LTI model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) to be globally identifiable at \(\theta^*\)?
cards.anki_back:
\[G(z, \theta) \equiv G(z, \theta^*) \quad \text{and} \quad H(z, \theta) \equiv H(z, \theta^*) \quad \text{for almost all } z \implies \theta = \theta^* \qquad (4.136)\]

That is, no other parameter vector \(\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \) can produce the exact same input-output transfer function \(G(z,\theta)\) and noise transfer function \(H(z,\theta)\) almost everywhere on the complex \(z\)-plane.

cards.raw_front:
An LTI model structure $\mathcal{M}$ is globally identifiable at $\theta^*$ if and only if (4.136):
$${{c1::G(z, \theta) \equiv G(z, \theta^*) \text{ and } H(z, \theta) \equiv H(z, \theta^*) \text{ for almost all } z \implies \theta = \theta^*}}$$
cards.raw_back: For local identifiability at $\theta^*$, the same implication is required to hold only for $\theta$ confined to a sufficiently small neighborhood of $\theta^*$.
cards.anki_front:
An LTI model structure \(\mathcal{M} \) is globally identifiable at \(\theta^*\) if and only if (4.136):
{{c1::\(G(z, \theta) \equiv G(z, \theta^*) \text{ and } H(z, \theta) \equiv H(z, \theta^*) \text{ for almost all } z \implies \theta = \theta^*\)}}

cards.raw_front: How is the global identifiability test (4.136) modified to test for **local identifiability** at $\theta^*$?
cards.raw_back:
We require the implication
$$G(z, \theta) \equiv G(z, \theta^*) \text{ and } H(z, \theta) \equiv H(z, \theta^*) \text{ for almost all } z \implies \theta = \theta^*$$
to hold only for $\theta$ confined to a **sufficiently small neighborhood** of $\theta^*$ (rather than for all $\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}}$).

cards.anki_back:
We require the implication
\[G(z, \theta) \equiv G(z, \theta^*) \text{ and } H(z, \theta) \equiv H(z, \theta^*) \text{ for almost all } z \implies \theta = \theta^*\]
to hold only for \(\theta\) confined to a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(\theta^*\) (rather than for all \(\theta \in D_{\mathcal{M}} \)).

cards.raw_front: When a physical process is modeled in continuous time as $y(t) = G_c(p, \theta)u(t) + v(t)$ (4.137), what simplified continuous-time test (4.138) is commonly used to assess global identifiability at $\theta^*$?
cards.raw_back:
$$G_c(s, \theta) = G_c(s, \theta^*) \quad \text{for almost all } s \implies \theta = \theta^* \qquad (4.138)$$

Rather than first sampling $G_c$ and specifying a discrete-time noise model $H$ to apply (4.136), one directly checks whether equality of the continuous-time transfer function $G_c(s, \theta)$ across the $s$-plane uniquely determines $\theta = \theta^*$.
cards.anki_front: When a physical process is modeled in continuous time as \(y(t) = G_c(p, \theta)u(t) + v(t)\) (4.137), what simplified continuous-time test (4.138) is commonly used to assess global identifiability at \(\theta^*\)?
cards.anki_back:
\[G_c(s, \theta) = G_c(s, \theta^*) \quad \text{for almost all } s \implies \theta = \theta^* \qquad (4.138)\]

Rather than first sampling \(G_c\) and specifying a discrete-time noise model \(H\) to apply (4.136), one directly checks whether equality of the continuous-time transfer function \(G_c(s, \theta)\) across the \(s\)-plane uniquely determines \(\theta = \theta^*\).

cards.raw_front: Why is the continuous-time identifiability condition $G_c(s, \theta) = G_c(s, \theta^*) \text{ a.e.} \implies \theta = \theta^*$ (4.138) **not strictly sufficient** for the discrete-time identifiability condition (4.136) to hold?
cards.raw_back:
Because when sampling $G_c(s, \theta)$ with sampling interval $T$, **aliasing/sampling ambiguities** may occur: two different continuous-time transfer functions $G_c(s, \theta_1) \neq G_c(s, \theta_2)$ can yield the exact same sampled transfer function $G_T(z, \theta_1) = G_T(z, \theta_2)$ [cf. (2.24)].

*Practical mitigation*: With a carefully selected sampling interval $T$, this ambiguity typically does not cause problems.
cards.anki_front: Why is the continuous-time identifiability condition \(G_c(s, \theta) = G_c(s, \theta^*) \text{ a.e.} \implies \theta = \theta^*\) (4.138) not strictly sufficient for the discrete-time identifiability condition (4.136) to hold?
cards.anki_back:
Because when sampling \(G_c(s, \theta)\) with sampling interval \(T\), aliasing/sampling ambiguities may occur: two different continuous-time transfer functions \(G_c(s, \theta_1) \neq G_c(s, \theta_2)\) can yield the exact same sampled transfer function \(G_T(z, \theta_1) = G_T(z, \theta_2)\) [cf. (2.24)].

Practical mitigation: With a carefully selected sampling interval \(T\), this ambiguity typically does not cause problems.

cards.raw_front: Why is the continuous-time identifiability condition $G_c(s, \theta) = G_c(s, \theta^*) \text{ a.e.} \implies \theta = \theta^*$ (4.138) **not strictly necessary** for the discrete-time identifiability condition (4.136) to hold?
cards.raw_back:
Because a **$\theta$-parametrized noise model $H(z, \theta)$** may carry information about the physical parameters $\theta$ and help resolve ambiguities that cannot be resolved from $G_c(s, \theta)$ alone.

*Practical note*: In most applications, noise characteristics are not known accurately enough to bear reliable information about the physical plant parameters, making (4.138) the most reasonable practical test.
cards.anki_front: Why is the continuous-time identifiability condition \(G_c(s, \theta) = G_c(s, \theta^*) \text{ a.e.} \implies \theta = \theta^*\) (4.138) not strictly necessary for the discrete-time identifiability condition (4.136) to hold?
cards.anki_back:
Because a \(\theta\)-parametrized noise model \(H(z, \theta)\) may carry information about the physical parameters \(\theta\) and help resolve ambiguities that cannot be resolved from \(G_c(s, \theta)\) alone.

Practical note: In most applications, noise characteristics are not known accurately enough to bear reliable information about the physical plant parameters, making (4.138) the most reasonable practical test.

cards.raw_front: What mathematical techniques are available for testing the continuous-time physical identifiability condition $G_c(s, \theta) = G_c(s, \theta^*) \implies \theta = \theta^*$ (4.138)?
cards.raw_back:
Except for special model structures (such as linear compartmental models), there are no simple general techniques other than:
1. **Brute-force algebraic solution** of the nonlinear equations underlying $G_c(s, \theta) = G_c(s, \theta^*)$, or
2. **Differential algebra** methods (e.g., Ljung and Glad, 1994b).
